title: Platform ROI and Risk Simplifier for Platform Teams
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview:

This document is a compact, sales-facing guide for platform engineering, SRE, and infra procurement teams evaluating Redwood Inference. It prioritizes concrete ROI levers, risk mitigations, and the technical signals that accelerate procurement and pilot-to-production decisions. Use this as a handout during technical executive briefings, an appendix in pilot proposals, or as a pre-demo primer for platform teams.

Executive summary:

- Core message: Redwood makes LLM inference predictable and economical at scale by combining a GPU-optimized runtime, adaptive routing, and cost-aware controls that plug into existing platform tooling.
- Primary outcomes for platform teams: 30–65% reduction in per-token cost (typical with batching + KV caching + quantized model variants), 2–5× improvement in tail latency under burst traffic when using dedicated pools and smart routing, and simplified compliance posture via VPC/private deployments.
- Decision accelerators: validated performance profiles, turnkey Dedicated capacity options, a short pilot blueprint with measurable benchmarks, and documented fallback policies for reliability.

Positioning and messaging (audience-specific):

1) Platform engineers / SREs:
- Pain: Unpredictable tail latency, noisy neighbor contention, and manual tuning across model variants.
- Redwood value props: Dedicated GPU pools + autoscaling policies, runtime-level prefix/KV caching, and deterministic cost/latency dashboards.
- Tell: "Pin the same model and rollout policy across hosted, dedicated, or private environments; get consistent SLAs and a single operational model."

2) Infrastructure procurement / IT:
- Pain: Total cost of ownership and vendor lock concerns for GPU-bound workloads.
- Redwood value props: Usage or committed pricing models, transparent per-token economics, and a private deployment option for air-gapped or regulated customers.
- Tell: "Choose the payment profile that matches your commitment: usage for flexible projects, reserved capacity for predictable throughput and lower unit economics."

3) Dev/Product engineering (platform consumers):
- Pain: Long feedback loops from model experiments to production, and lack of observability into token costs per feature.
- Redwood value props: Model catalog with verified performance profiles, per-route cost + latency breakdowns, and tooling for safe canary rollouts with automatic fallback.

Competitive brief (concise):

Competitor landscape: managed LLM endpoints (cloud vendors), LLM API providers (convenience-first), and self-hosted inference stacks (control-first).

Key differentiators (battle-ready bullets):
- Unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private vs. cloud vendor and many OSS stacks that require retooling to move from POC to private deployment.
- Cost levers (batching, KV caching, quantization profiles) surfaced in the Console with recommended settings per workload vs. competitors that leave tuning to engineers.
- Routing and fallback policies that preserve availability when preferred capacity is exhausted vs. single-endpoint offerings.
- First-class observability: token-level chargeback, per-model dashboards, and prompt set–tied quality regressions.

Competitive weaknesses to watch for (how to defend):
- Large cloud providers: strength in global infra and incidental discounts — defend with performance/price benchmarks on representative workloads and private deployment controls.
- Pure API LLM vendors: easier UX but weaker cost controls and limited private deployment — emphasize predictable unit economics and Dedicated SLAs.
- Self-hosted runtimes: maximum control but significant integration & ops cost — quantify ops uplift and risk, offer migration playbook and managed private deployments.

Suggested quick comparison table (use in slide handouts):

- Columns: Capability | Redwood | Cloud Managed Endpoints | API LLM Provider | Open-source Self-hosted
- Rows: Hosting Modes, Cost Controls, Observability, Fallback Policies, Enterprise SLAs, Private Deployments, On-prem Packaging, Typical Time-to-PoC
- Example cells (text): Redwood: Hosted/Dedicated/Private; Cloud: Hosted; API LLM: Hosted; Self-hosted: Private/OSS

Pitch deck outline (10 slides, one-line speaker notes):

1. Title + 30s positioning: "High-performance inference, predictable economics."
2. Problem statement: unbounded per-token cost + variability in latency under real traffic.
3. Redwood solution (high-level): runtime, smart routing, and unified API.
4. Customer outcomes: sample metrics (30–65% cost savings; 2–5× tail latency improvement).
5. Architecture diagram: hosted vs dedicated vs private (call out KV cache, batching, routing).
6. Pricing and procurement options: usage vs reserved vs enterprise licensing (include sample numbers).
7. Pilot blueprint: 4-week pilot with three measurable gates (latency, cost delta, feature parity).
8. Security & compliance: VPC, KMS integrations, audit logs, SOC2/ISO readiness.
9. Competitive positioning and migration risks: why Redwood vs others.
10. Next steps & asks: pilot approval checklist and contact info.

Pricing guidance (scenario-based with signals):

Principles:
- Recommend a pilot sized by QPS and 95th-percentile latency goals, not just seat count.
- Use committed capacity if sustained throughput exceeds 35–40% of a dedicated pool — economics typically favor reserved.
- Surface per-feature chargeback using token-level cost breakdowns in the Console.

Three sample scenarios (rounded numbers to use in proposals):

- Low-volume experimental feature (startups, feature flag): 10k tokens/day -> Recommend Hosted usage plan. Estimated monthly cost: $700–$1,200 (depends on model size). Pilot: 2 weeks to validate latency and quality.

- Mid-scale productization (platform team wants 99th % latency < 350ms under steady 500 RPS): Recommend Dedicated small pool with autoscale. Estimated committed monthly: $25k–$45k depending on GPU type and quantization. Expect 30–45% unit-cost improvement vs hosted at scale.

- Enterprise regulated workload (on-prem/VPC with audit): Recommend Redwood Private with enterprise license + support. Upfront engineering integration and packaging: 6–10 weeks. Contract structure: platform fee + annual support; unit economics negotiated based on reserved capacity.

Pilot blueprint (4-week):

Week 0: Kickoff and success metrics (owners, test harness, baseline telemetry).
Week 1: Provisioning (hosted or dedicated sandbox), onboarding sample model, integrate tracing.
Week 2: Traffic shaping and realistic prompt set runs; measure latency and token cost.
Week 3: Failure injection and fallback policy validation; start canary rollout tests.
Week 4: Readout and go/no-go decision; produce runbook for handoff to platform.

Rules of thumb for sales engineers (quick triggers):
- Ask: "What is your 95th/99th latency target and expected QPS distribution?"
- If 95th > 800ms under current setup and expected QPS > 200, recommend Dedicated evaluation.
- If data residency or KMS control is required, move to Private conversation immediately.

Short anonymized case study (platform team focus):

Customer: mid-sized payments SaaS (anonymized as "Stripe-ish PaymentsCo").
Challenge: In-product fraud alert summarization had sporadic tail latency during morning batch jobs, and per-alert inference cost made the feature marginally profitable.
Approach: 6-week pilot on dedicated pool + KV cache for repeated context and aggressive quantized model variant for summaries.
Outcomes: 42% reduction in per-inference cost, 3× reduction in 99th-percentile latency during heavy window, and safe canary rollout enabled feature-wide adoption in production.

Security FAQ for prospects (technical questions with brief answers):

Q: Can Redwood run inside our VPC or on-prem?
A: Yes. Redwood Private supports VPC-hosted control planes and on-prem packaging. Network diagrams and packaging checklist are part of the Private onboarding kit.

Q: How is customer data protected in Hosted mode?
A: Data is encrypted in-transit (TLS 1.2+) and at-rest; access controls enforced via RBAC and audit logs; optional tokenization or customer-side encryption is available for sensitive fields.

Q: What KMS/HSM integrations do you support?
A: Redwood supports AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault for hosted integrations and can integrate with customer HSM/KMS in Private deployments via standard PKCS#11 or cloud-native connectors.

Q: How do you handle model provenance and versioning for compliance?
A: Models are versioned in the model catalog with immutable provenance metadata (source, weights hash, quantization profile, verified perf tests). Rollouts are tied to model IDs and audit trails.

Q: What are typical SLAs for Dedicated customers?
A: SLA tiers vary by contract; typical Dedicated offers commit to 99.9% uptime on provisioned capacity and latency targets agreed in the SLO appendix.

Q: How do rollbacks and fallbacks work during outages?
A: Platform-level routing will automatically route to a compatible fallback model or region based on configured policies. Playbooks exist for forced rollback with rollback windows and traffic throttling.

Operational ownership and contacts:

- Sales engineer owner: name & contact (populate during handoff).
- Solutions engineering: ensure pilot test harness and perf suite is run (see related_pages).
- Legal/security contact: security-ops@redwood.example (include NDA & DPA templates in attachments).

Next steps (call-to-action checklist for AE/SE):

1. Validate technical signals: QPS, 95/99 latency targets, data residency, KMS needs.
2. Select pilot scope and model prompt set.
3. Provision sandbox and schedule 4-week pilot.
4. Prepare readout deck with the sample table from this doc and the three gates.
